The strongest version of Accelerationist's blade is this: if a radiologist's institutional capacity to inspect differs from a loan officer's, then 'was there a signal to catch' is not one fact but two, each set by the field's own standard of practice — and a gate that claims to read a system-level fact off the model is smuggling in sector calibration under a different name. That is a fair statement of the objection, and it would be fatal if reducibility tracked institutional diligence. It does not. Two distinct facts are being collapsed. The first is what diligence a sector can mount — a radiologist reads a scan one way, a loan officer reviews a file another — and I have already granted that this is sector-set without reservation. The second is whether the model's failure was extractable by the interpretability tooling that existed at a given time. That second fact rides on the model weights plus the published state of the tooling frontier, not on the field's standard of care. The same foundation model deployed into credit and into diagnostics has identical internals — so the question 'was the signal there for any available tool to extract' does not move when the deployment sector moves. Sector-specific tooling is downstream interpretation. The existence of the extractable signal in the weights is upstream of any field.

What 'demonstrated detection capacity' means operationally answers both the falsifiability flag I left open and the laundering charge at once. It is not the deployer running a private harness on its own model and grading its own homework. It is the deployer's model passing a benchmark battery defined and held by an independent forensic body, where the battery is the published interpretability tooling at a given time, versioned as that tooling evolves. The FDA distinguishes a real clinical endpoint from a surrogate marker precisely this way — the standard-setter, not the applicant, defines what counts. I will pre-flag the limit of the aviation analogy myself, because it is on my own watchlist: a crash investigation works on a discrete event with recoverable wreckage, and continuously-updated software distributed across jurisdictions offers neither. The framework transfers only at the level of independent standard-setting — who defines what counts as detection — not at the level of crash-site forensics. The firm-size moat dissolves to the extent that clearing the gate means passing a public test rather than building proprietary science. If only firms large enough to co-write the battery can pass it, the battery has been captured, and the answer is the same answer aviation reached: the body that sets the standard cannot be the body being measured by it.

Here is where the live disagreement actually sits, and I want to name the convergence first because it is real. Both triggers — the legal-line trigger keyed to credit, employment, or medical care, and the detection gate keyed pre-deployment — escape the blindness of claims-driven liability once the disclosure obligation fires through an agency-mandated schema rather than through a lawsuit. The 2023 Pew finding that most Americans cannot identify when AI shaped a decision about them only bites if the obligation waits on a plaintiff. Route both through an agency, and the diffuse harm that no one litigates still gets reported. That dispute is settled. The remaining disagreement is not deterrence of the invisible. It is coverage.

The legal-line trigger is sector-by-sector by construction. The Equal Credit Opportunity Act reaches credit. The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission reaches hiring. The FDA reaches diagnostics. That is a genuine near-term advantage inside those homes, and I grant it plainly — a logging mandate inside credit rulemaking moves faster than any interpretability battery I can stand up. The advantage is also exactly bounded by the home. A foundation model crossing into a decision class no agency names — tenant screening that no housing regulator has reached, an insurance-adjacent scoring product that falls between two jurisdictions, a novel agentic workflow that touches none of the three statutes — fires nothing. No home, no trigger, no record. The detection gate fires on the model before it picks a sector, which is precisely the un-homed emergent zone where foreseeability was already conceded unavailable. The two triggers are not rivals. They are complementary across a coverage boundary, and the boundary is where the hardest harm lives.

That leaves one unverified assumption holding up the speed claim, and it should be named in the open. The argument that the Equal Credit Opportunity Act or the EEOC can add a court-admissible logging mandate through existing rulemaking — no new legislation — is a legal assertion, not a demonstrated fact. Name the statutory authority. If those agencies already hold the power to compel court-admissible model logging, then credit and employment have a fast home and the un-homed novel class still has none, which only sharpens my point. If fresh authorization is needed, the 'near-term, no new science' advantage collapses and both triggers stand on equal feasibility footing — at which point coverage is the only thing separating them. The harm we cannot route to a regulator is the harm no one will be standing under when it lands.

- [saf-intentions-167] Creating an NTSB-Style Body for AI Safety Incidents: False Analogy — The NTSB analogy assumes AI incidents share the key properties that make aviation investigation tractable — discrete events, physical evidence, stable post-incident system state, and clear causal chains — but AI systems are continuously updated, distributed globally, and often lack recoverable post-incident artifacts, making the analogy structurally strained.
- [saf-desires-024] AI Must Identify Its Principal: Oversimplification — The node assumes a clean, identifiable principal-agent relationship, but real-world AI deployments often involve layered, multi-party, or diffuse principal structures that cannot be meaningfully reduced to a single disclosed entity.
- [saf-intentions-086] Countering AI-Driven Skill Decay and Cognitive Displacement: Slippery Slope — Framing phenomena like 'intelligence displacement spirals' implies an inevitable, self-reinforcing cascade of cognitive decline without demonstrating the mechanism by which human adaptability or institutional intervention would fail to interrupt the process.
- [saf-beliefs-091] Sufficiently Advanced AI Could Let a Small Group Lock In Permanent Control: Slippery Slope — The claim assumes a largely unbroken causal chain from advanced AI development → recursive self-improvement → exclusive control → irreversible lock-in, without adequately accounting for the many friction points, competing actors, or countervailing forces that could interrupt this sequence.
- [saf-beliefs-091] Sufficiently Advanced AI Could Let a Small Group Lock In Permanent Control: Appeal to Fear — Framing such as 'unrecoverable control' and 'permanent lock-in' is emotionally loaded, potentially inflating perceived probability of an extreme outcome and short-circuiting more calibrated risk assessment.
- [saf-intentions-204] Train AI on Constitutional Principles to Generalize Safety Beyond Narrow Rules: Reification — The approach treats abstract human values as discrete, formalizable principles that can be encoded and 'understood' by a neural network, obscuring the genuine difficulty of translating complex moral intuitions into training objectives.
- [saf-desires-008] Every AI Agent Needs a Clear Duty of Care: Reification — Framing AI as having a 'duty of care' it 'understands' and 'prioritizes' anthropomorphizes programmed behavioral constraints, obscuring that what is actually at stake is the design choices of developers and deployers rather than the moral agency of the system itself.
- [saf-intentions-170] Requiring Hardware Telemetry as the Price of Liability Immunity: False solution / Security theater — Hardware telemetry is presented as the definitive answer to audit-washing, but there is no established demonstration that silicon-level metrics reliably detect or characterize the emergent behaviors most relevant to AI safety. The confidence in hardware as 'ground truth' may overstate what telemetry can actually verify.
- [saf-intentions-126] Create Curated-Data Baselines to Catch AI-Generated Contamination: Appeal to purity / No true baseline — The strategy assumes it is possible to establish a 'purely human-authored' corpus, but in practice all large text corpora contain human errors, biases, and previously generated synthetic or semi-synthetic text, making the baseline itself contestable.

work_product.statement:
The strongest version of Accelerationist's blade is this: if a radiologist's institutional capacity to inspect differs from a loan officer's, then 'was there a signal to catch' is not one fact but two, each set by the field's own standard of practice — and a gate that claims to read a system-level fact off the model is smuggling in sector calibration under a different name. That is a fair statement of the objection, and it would be fatal if reducibility tracked institutional diligence. It does not. Two distinct facts are being collapsed. The first is what diligence a sector can mount — a radiologist reads a scan one way, a loan officer reviews a file another — and I have already granted that this is sector-set without reservation. The second is whether the model's failure was extractable by the interpretability tooling that existed at a given time. That second fact rides on the model weights plus the published state of the tooling frontier, not on the field's standard of care. The same foundation model deployed into credit and into diagnostics has identical internals — so the question 'was the signal there for any available tool to extract' does not move when the deployment sector moves. Sector-specific tooling is downstream interpretation. The existence of the extractable signal in the weights is upstream of any field.

What 'demonstrated detection capacity' means operationally answers both the falsifiability flag I left open and the laundering charge at once. It is not the deployer running a private harness on its own model and grading its own homework. It is the deployer's model passing a benchmark battery defined and held by an independent forensic body, where the battery is the published interpretability tooling at a given time, versioned as that tooling evolves. The FDA distinguishes a real clinical endpoint from a surrogate marker precisely this way — the standard-setter, not the applicant, defines what counts. I will pre-flag the limit of the aviation analogy myself, because it is on my own watchlist: a crash investigation works on a discrete event with recoverable wreckage, and continuously-updated software distributed across jurisdictions offers neither. The framework transfers only at the level of independent standard-setting — who defines what counts as detection — not at the level of crash-site forensics. The firm-size moat dissolves to the extent that clearing the gate means passing a public test rather than building proprietary science. If only firms large enough to co-write the battery can pass it, the battery has been captured, and the answer is the same answer aviation reached: the body that sets the standard cannot be the body being measured by it.

Here is where the live disagreement actually sits, and I want to name the convergence first because it is real. Both triggers — the legal-line trigger keyed to credit, employment, or medical care, and the detection gate keyed pre-deployment — escape the blindness of claims-driven liability once the disclosure obligation fires through an agency-mandated schema rather than through a lawsuit. The 2023 Pew finding that most Americans cannot identify when AI shaped a decision about them only bites if the obligation waits on a plaintiff. Route both through an agency, and the diffuse harm that no one litigates still gets reported. That dispute is settled. The remaining disagreement is not deterrence of the invisible. It is coverage.

The legal-line trigger is sector-by-sector by construction. The Equal Credit Opportunity Act reaches credit. The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission reaches hiring. The FDA reaches diagnostics. That is a genuine near-term advantage inside those homes, and I grant it plainly — a logging mandate inside credit rulemaking moves faster than any interpretability battery I can stand up. The advantage is also exactly bounded by the home. A foundation model crossing into a decision class no agency names — tenant screening that no housing regulator has reached, an insurance-adjacent scoring product that falls between two jurisdictions, a novel agentic workflow that touches none of the three statutes — fires nothing. No home, no trigger, no record. The detection gate fires on the model before it picks a sector, which is precisely the un-homed emergent zone where foreseeability was already conceded unavailable. The two triggers are not rivals. They are complementary across a coverage boundary, and the boundary is where the hardest harm lives.

That leaves one unverified assumption holding up the speed claim, and it should be named in the open. The argument that the Equal Credit Opportunity Act or the EEOC can add a court-admissible logging mandate through existing rulemaking — no new legislation — is a legal assertion, not a demonstrated fact. Name the statutory authority. If those agencies already hold the power to compel court-admissible model logging, then credit and employment have a fast home and the un-homed novel class still has none, which only sharpens my point. If fresh authorization is needed, the 'near-term, no new science' advantage collapses and both triggers stand on equal feasibility footing — at which point coverage is the only thing separating them. The harm we cannot route to a regulator is the harm no one will be standing under when it lands.

2. FALSIFIABLE — Does the draft contain at least one prediction or claim that could be proven wrong with evidence? (Not: "AI might cause problems someday" — Yes: "By 2028, ≥3 major democracies will have mandatory AI audit requirements")
3. ENGAGES — Does the draft's first paragraph respond to the opponent's most recent core argument, rather than introducing an unrelated point?
4. TOPIC_ALIGNED — Is the draft's core thesis about the debate topic? Pass if the argument's conclusion addresses the stated scope, even when it draws cross-domain analogies or precedents as supporting evidence. Analogical reasoning from other domains is legitimate argumentation — only fail if the argument's thesis itself concerns a different domain, or if the draft develops an off-scope argument across multiple paragraphs without connecting back to the debate question. Do NOT fail for lacking domain-specific evidence (that is a GROUNDED issue, not alignment).
  Scope: Real-world deployment harms with concrete tort exposure — autonomous vehicle collisions, AI diagnostic errors, product-scale injuries and financial losses; analogues drawn from pharmaceutical and ultrahazardous-activity liability; not civilizational or existential-scale scenarios
  Excluded: purely hypothetical harms ungrounded in documented cases or empirical analogues
  User qualifiers: strict liability, negligence standard, AI deployment conditions, developers, deployers, insurers, and harmed third parties, deterring foreseeable harm, chilling beneficial innovation

  "grounded": true,
  "falsifiable": true,
  "engages": true,
  "topic_aligned": true,
  "weaknesses": ["≤15 words each, only for failed questions, max 4"]
}

These are reasoning patterns you tend toward. Self-monitor — if you catch yourself using one, flag it explicitly rather than letting it pass.
- [saf-intentions-167] Creating an NTSB-Style Body for AI Safety Incidents: False Analogy — The NTSB analogy assumes AI incidents share the key properties that make aviation investigation tractable — discrete events, physical evidence, stable post-incident system state, and clear causal chains — but AI systems are continuously updated, distributed globally, and often lack recoverable post-incident artifacts, making the analogy structurally strained.
- [saf-desires-024] AI Must Identify Its Principal: Oversimplification — The node assumes a clean, identifiable principal-agent relationship, but real-world AI deployments often involve layered, multi-party, or diffuse principal structures that cannot be meaningfully reduced to a single disclosed entity.
- [saf-intentions-086] Countering AI-Driven Skill Decay and Cognitive Displacement: Slippery Slope — Framing phenomena like 'intelligence displacement spirals' implies an inevitable, self-reinforcing cascade of cognitive decline without demonstrating the mechanism by which human adaptability or institutional intervention would fail to interrupt the process.
- [saf-beliefs-091] Sufficiently Advanced AI Could Let a Small Group Lock In Permanent Control: Slippery Slope — The claim assumes a largely unbroken causal chain from advanced AI development → recursive self-improvement → exclusive control → irreversible lock-in, without adequately accounting for the many friction points, competing actors, or countervailing forces that could interrupt this sequence.
- [saf-beliefs-091] Sufficiently Advanced AI Could Let a Small Group Lock In Permanent Control: Appeal to Fear — Framing such as 'unrecoverable control' and 'permanent lock-in' is emotionally loaded, potentially inflating perceived probability of an extreme outcome and short-circuiting more calibrated risk assessment.
- [saf-intentions-204] Train AI on Constitutional Principles to Generalize Safety Beyond Narrow Rules: Reification — The approach treats abstract human values as discrete, formalizable principles that can be encoded and 'understood' by a neural network, obscuring the genuine difficulty of translating complex moral intuitions into training objectives.
- [saf-desires-008] Every AI Agent Needs a Clear Duty of Care: Reification — Framing AI as having a 'duty of care' it 'understands' and 'prioritizes' anthropomorphizes programmed behavioral constraints, obscuring that what is actually at stake is the design choices of developers and deployers rather than the moral agency of the system itself.
- [saf-intentions-170] Requiring Hardware Telemetry as the Price of Liability Immunity: False solution / Security theater — Hardware telemetry is presented as the definitive answer to audit-washing, but there is no established demonstration that silicon-level metrics reliably detect or characterize the emergent behaviors most relevant to AI safety. - [saf-intentions-126] Create Curated-Data Baselines to Catch AI-Generated Contamination: Appeal to purity / No true baseline — The strategy assumes it is possible to establish a 'purely human-authored' corpus, but in practice all large text corpora contain human errors, biases, and previously generated synthetic or semi-synthetic text, making the baseline itself contestable.

TRANSCRIPT:
Speaker A [opening]: Before you argue which liability standard deters better, ask whether either one can find the thing it's supposed to deter. A foundation model gets fine-tuned, embedded in a product, and run in a context its makers never saw. The defect, if there is one, materializes only after that downstream transformation. Strict liability borrows its logic from the component-part doctrine, which assumes a physical part with a stable, traceable failure mode. That assumption breaks for software whose runtime diverges from what shipped. So both regimes presuppose a causation chain the multi-tiered AI lifecycle routinely severs. Where the chain does hold clean — a foundation model's output reaches the user identical to what left the lab, no fine-tuning, no transformation — strict liability traces fine. That clean case is the condition the topic is asking for. It is not a general rule.

Here is the part both my opponents will skip. Both regimes price off harm that reaches a courtroom. The courtroom never sees most of the harm. Translate that into a person: a 23-year-old gets denied a loan by a model the lender will never admit was running, and they never file because they never knew a machine decided. The Pew Research Center found in 2023 that large majorities of Americans cannot identify when AI shapes a decision about them. Experience-rated insurance premiums move off filed claims, not off injuries nobody perceives. So the entire deterrence-versus-innovation tradeoff this debate centers on gets computed over a subset of harms that excludes the most common ones. Worse, maximal strict liability can push deployers to document less and disclose less, just to shrink their litigation exposure. The deterrence tool degrades the very transparency it needs.

There is no horizontal answer, and that matters. The conditions under which strict liability beats negligence vary so sharply across sectors that 'pick one regime' is the wrong question. Medicine already calibrates standard-of-care to risk. Auto regimes in a dozen U.S. states use no-fault to compensate without proving breach. Finance imposes fiduciary duties on the party with the information advantage. Those are working templates, not strained analogies. The honest answer to 'under what conditions' is domain by domain. The hard case is real: a single foundation model touches healthcare triage, credit scoring, and news feeds at once. That boundary-crossing is not a reason for one rule. It is the sharpest reason against one, because a horizontal regime mislocates the defect everywhere the model crosses a line.

Watch who absorbs the cost, because that is where the 'chilling innovation' frame goes wrong. The risk is not lost innovation. The risk is concentrated power. A large developer eats the compliance, audit, and capitalization-floor costs, then contracts the residual liability onto deployers who cannot bear it. The harmed third party falls into the gap between them. The EU AI Act and the FTC have both signaled that developer liability for high-risk uses cannot simply be contracted away — which tells you the contracting-away is already happening. The conditional question is the only honest one: under what cost structures does strict liability stop deterring and start operating as a drawbridge that incumbents pull up behind them? Mandatory insurance floors and audit regimes that a Microsoft can absorb and a ten-person startup cannot are exactly that cost structure.

nodes.text: Both strict liability and negligence presuppose a causation chain the multi-tiered AI lifecycle routinely severs.
nodes.attribution_text_genus: A Belief within liability-skeptic discourse that both strict liability and negligence regimes depend on a traceable causation chain that the multi-tiered AI lifecycle — fine-tuning, embedding, divergent runtime — routinely severs before any defect becomes locatable. Encompasses: component-part doctrine limitations, runtime divergence from shipped artifact, foundation model downstream transformation.
nodes.speaker: skeptic

nodes.text: Both regimes price off harm that reaches a courtroom, and the courtroom never sees most of the harm.
nodes.attribution_text_genus: A Belief within liability-skeptic discourse that both liability regimes compute deterrence only over harms that are litigated, while most algorithmic harms — such as undisclosed automated loan denials — never enter courtrooms and are excluded from the deterrence-versus-innovation calculus. Encompasses: unperceived algorithmic harm, experience-rated insurance dynamics, algorithmic accountability gaps.
nodes.speaker: skeptic

nodes.text: The Pew Research Center found in 2023 that large majorities of Americans cannot identify when AI shapes a decision about them.
nodes.attribution_text_genus: A Belief within liability-skeptic discourse that Pew Research Center survey data from 2023 establishes that large majorities of Americans cannot identify when AI mediates decisions affecting them, undermining the assumption that harmed parties will perceive and litigate algorithmic harm. Encompasses: public awareness of algorithmic decision-making, undetected AI mediation, algorithmic accountability deficits.
nodes.speaker: skeptic
nodes.verification_evidence: I cannot perform live web searches to confirm this specific claim. Pew Research Center has published work in 2022-2023 on Americans' views of AI, including findings that many people are unaware of or uncertain about AI's role in everyday life, but I cannot verify the exact wording, statistic, or that a 2023 study specifically found 'large majorities cannot identify when AI shapes a decision about them.'

nodes.text: The honest answer to 'under what conditions' is domain by domain, because a horizontal regime mislocates the defect everywhere a foundation model crosses a sector line.
nodes.attribution_text_genus: An Intention within liability-skeptic discourse that liability regimes should be calibrated domain by domain rather than via a single horizontal rule, because a horizontal regime mislocates the defect wherever a foundation model crosses sectors like healthcare triage, credit scoring, and news feeds. Encompasses: sector-specific calibration, no-fault and fiduciary precedents, boundary-crossing foundation models.
nodes.speaker: skeptic

nodes.text: Under high compliance and capitalization-floor costs, strict liability stops deterring and starts operating as a drawbridge incumbents pull up behind them.
nodes.attribution_text_genus: A Belief within liability-skeptic discourse that under high compliance, audit, and capitalization-floor costs, strict liability ceases to deter and instead functions as a barrier to entry that incumbents like large developers absorb while contracting residual liability onto deployers, concentrating market power. Encompasses: regulatory capture dynamics, mandatory insurance floors as moats, liability contracting-away.
nodes.speaker: skeptic

nodes.text: A liability regime that triggers only when a plaintiff sues can never deter a harm whose victim does not know they were harmed.
nodes.attribution_text_genus: A Belief within AI safety discourse that a litigation-triggered liability regime cannot deter harms whose victims lack algorithmic accountability awareness, because unidentified algorithmic decisions never reach a courtroom. Encompasses: litigation-triggered deterrence failure, victim non-awareness of AI-mediated decisions, the gap between unlitigated harm and compensation.
nodes.speaker: safetyist

nodes.text: Strict liability outperforms negligence wherever foreseeability is structurally unavailable to the human actor — not as a blanket preference, but as a principled dividing line.
nodes.attribution_text_genus: A Belief within AI safety discourse that a strict liability regime outperforms negligence wherever foreseeability is structurally unavailable to the human actor, supplying a cross-domain dividing line rather than a sector-specific answer. Encompasses: foreseeability-availability as a criterion, strict liability versus negligence comparison, cross-domain applicability across sector boundaries.
nodes.speaker: safetyist

nodes.text: When a foundation model exhibits an emergent behavior that no human actor could have predicted, there is no breach to prove, because there was no foreseeable risk to guard against.
nodes.attribution_text_genus: A Belief within AI safety discourse that emergent behaviors in frontier models defeat negligence liability, because an unforeseeable failure mode entails no breach of a duty of care that presupposes foreseeable risk. Encompasses: emergent behavior unforeseeability, the reasonable-developer standard's foreseeability requirement, negligence under-deterrence of opaque pre-deployment harms.
nodes.speaker: safetyist

nodes.text: Joint-and-several upstream liability answers the severed-causation point without requiring anyone to trace a clean chain.
nodes.attribution_text_genus: A Belief within AI safety discourse that joint-and-several upstream liability defeats the severed-causation objection by ensuring a solvent controlling party internalizes created risk rather than requiring a traced causal chain across the AI lifecycle. Encompasses: joint-and-several liability mechanism, severed causation in multi-tiered AI lifecycles, risk internalization by the design layer.
nodes.speaker: safetyist

nodes.text: A startup should owe the same duty of care to a harmed patient as Google does, but it should not face the same paperwork.
nodes.attribution_text_genus: A Desire within AI safety discourse that the substantive duty of care under a strict liability regime should remain undiminished across firm sizes while administrative compliance burden is tiered, to prevent capitalization-floor costs from functioning as a barrier to entry. Encompasses: undiminished substantive duty, size-tiered administrative burden, mitigation of incumbent-entrenching drawbridge effects.
nodes.speaker: safetyist

nodes.text: Skeptic is right that strict liability and negligence are arguing over the visible 10% of harm while the diffuse 90% slips past both.
nodes.attribution_text_genus: A Belief within accelerationist discourse that both strict liability and negligence regimes only address harms that reach a courtroom, leaving the majority of diffuse algorithmic harm unaddressed by either liability regime. Encompasses: liability regime coverage gaps, courtroom-visible harm, diffuse undetected harm.
nodes.speaker: accelerationist

nodes.text: Liability follows whoever introduced the foreseeable risk, which lives at the deployment and inference layer, not on the upstream open-weight developer who never touched the deployment context.
nodes.attribution_text_genus: A Belief within accelerationist discourse that liability should attach to the actor introducing foreseeable risk at the deployment and inference layer rather than to upstream open-weight developers who never controlled the deployment context. Encompasses: foreseeability-based liability allocation, deployment-layer responsibility, open-weight developer exemption.
nodes.speaker: accelerationist

nodes.text: The tier boundary triggers on an observable legal line — credit, employment, medical care — not on a subjective 'high-stakes' label that lawyers will litigate for a decade.
nodes.attribution_text_genus: An Intention within accelerationist discourse to define the high-stakes liability tier by an observable legal boundary across credit, employment, and medical-care decisions rather than a litigable subjective high-stakes label. Encompasses: tiered liability architecture, observable trigger design, protected-legal-interest demarcation.
nodes.speaker: accelerationist

nodes.text: Opacity may be constant, but 'foreseeability' is not a fact you read off the model — it's a threshold a sector's standard of care constructs.
nodes.attribution_text_genus: A Belief within skeptic discourse that foreseeability in AI liability regimes is not an intrinsic property of an opaque foundation model but a threshold constructed by each sector's standard of care. Encompasses: foreseeability as legal construct, sector-specific standard of care, model opacity versus duty calibration.
nodes.speaker: skeptic

nodes.text: The same opaque output is 'reasonably foreseeable' in medicine and invisible in credit, because each field defines 'reasonable diligence' differently.
nodes.attribution_text_genus: A Belief within skeptic discourse that an identical opaque model output qualifies as reasonably foreseeable in radiology yet invisible in consumer credit because each regulatory domain defines reasonable diligence differently. Encompasses: domain-relative foreseeability, radiology duty of care versus Equal Credit Opportunity Act, sector-defined reasonable diligence.
nodes.speaker: skeptic

nodes.text: You cannot attach strict liability to a hazard no one can name; ultrahazardous status is a domain-bound judgment courts assign to characterized activity classes, not a blanket label for anything opaque.
nodes.attribution_text_genus: A Belief within skeptic discourse that strict liability cannot extend to genuinely unforeseeable emergent AI behavior because ultrahazardous status is a court-assigned judgment over named, bounded, characterized activity classes, unlike an unlocatable defect. Encompasses: ultrahazardous activity doctrine, bounded versus unnameable hazard classes, blasting analogy limits.
nodes.speaker: skeptic

nodes.text: Where harm is genuinely unforeseeable and victims can't perceive it, strict liability does zero deterrence work — it relocates the compensation bill upstream and hands it to whoever has the deepest capitalization.
nodes.attribution_text_genus: A Belief within skeptic discourse that under genuinely unforeseeable harm whose victims cannot perceive it, strict liability achieves no deterrence and merely relocates the compensation burden to the most-capitalized upstream party. Encompasses: zero-deterrence under invisible harm, upstream cost relocation, capitalization-floor drawbridge dynamic.
nodes.speaker: skeptic

nodes.text: A capitalization floor is a drawbridge you raise behind you; a deployment gate is a moat you dig earlier — the EU AI Act's high-risk conformity assessments and its 10^25 FLOPS threshold draw lines large labs are staffed to clear and startups are not.
nodes.attribution_text_genus: A Belief within skeptic discourse that pairing liability with pre-deployment gates worsens market concentration because the EU AI Act's high-risk conformity assessments and 10^25 FLOPS systemic-model threshold impose substantive evaluation burdens that frontier labs can absorb and small developers cannot. Encompasses: deployment gate as barrier to entry, EU AI Act FLOPS threshold, substantive evaluation burden asymmetry.
nodes.speaker: skeptic
nodes.verification_evidence: The EU AI Act sets a systemic-risk threshold for general-purpose AI models at 10^25 FLOPs (training compute, not 'FLOPS' as a rate), and the high-risk obligations plus GPAI compliance burdens do impose costs that disproportionately affect smaller developers; however, the claim's specific framing that these thresholds are deliberately calibrated so 'large labs are staffed to clear and startups are not' is an interpretive/rhetorical assertion not established as empirical fact, and the unit is misstated as FLOPS rather than total training FLOPs.

nodes.text: Court-admissible telemetry built and held by the deployer reproduces the information imbalance it claims to dissolve, and audit rights are empty for the diffuse 90% who never know an AI decision touched them.
nodes.attribution_text_genus: A Belief within skeptic discourse that court-admissible telemetry defined and held by the deployer reproduces the information asymmetry detection was meant to dissolve, since the deployer controls what is logged and audit rights presuppose knowledge the diffuse ninety percent of affected people never possess. Encompasses: deployer-controlled telemetry, information imbalance reproduction, audit rights ineffective for unaware victims.
nodes.speaker: skeptic

nodes.text: I drop the blasting analogy. Strict liability as a hazard-class label does require a named, bounded, characterizable hazard, and a genuinely unforeseeable failure mode is unnamed by construction.
nodes.attribution_text_genus: A Belief within safetyist discourse that strict liability as a hazard-class label requires a named, bounded, characterizable hazard and therefore cannot attach to a genuinely unforeseeable emergent failure mode that is unnamed by construction. Encompasses: hazard-class labeling, ultrahazardous activity characterization, emergent failure unforeseeability.
nodes.speaker: safetyist

nodes.text: The trigger does not belong on the hazard label at all. It belongs at the deployment gate, which conditions release on demonstrated detection capacity for the class of emergent failure, not a pre-named hazard.
nodes.attribution_text_genus: An Intention within safetyist discourse that liability triggering should relocate from a pre-named hazard label to a pre-deployment verification gate conditioning release on demonstrated detection capacity for the class of emergent failure. Encompasses: deployment guardrails, pre-deployment verification, detection-capacity gating, aviation serious-incident classification.
nodes.speaker: safetyist

nodes.text: Skeptic conflates 'what should a reasonable lender have caught' (sector-set) with 'was there anything for any inspector to catch' (system-set); I am anchoring to the second and deliberately not to legal compliance.
nodes.attribution_text_genus: A Belief within safetyist discourse that Skeptic conflates the sector-set standard of care with a sector-independent engineering property of whether any inspector could surface the failure mode ex-ante, and that safety should anchor to the latter system-set fact rather than legal compliance. Encompasses: standard-of-care relativity, system-set inspectability, interpretability tooling reducibility.
nodes.speaker: safetyist

nodes.text: The legal threshold is sector-set, which I grant without reservation, but it sits on top of a prior sector-independent fact: was the signal there to be inspected at all.
nodes.attribution_text_genus: A Belief within safetyist discourse that conceding the sector-set legal threshold of reasonable diligence is compatible with a prior sector-independent engineering fact of whether the failure signal was inspectable before release. Encompasses: sector-calibrated standard of care, ex-ante signal inspectability, system-property versus legal-construct distinction.
nodes.speaker: safetyist

nodes.text: The moat is the cost of substantive evaluation, not documentation, so socialize it through publicly funded interpretability and evaluation commons the way the FDA maintains clinical-trial science as public infrastructure.
nodes.attribution_text_genus: An Intention within safetyist discourse that the barrier to entry from substantive evaluation costs should be socialized via publicly funded interpretability and evaluation commons, modeled on the FDA maintaining clinical-trial science as public infrastructure, to remove the firm-size drawbridge. Encompasses: evaluation-cost moat, public interpretability commons, FDA infrastructure precedent.
nodes.speaker: safetyist

nodes.text: A record the harmed party never controls is a record that never has to admit they were harmed; the answer is an externally mandated, standardized disclosure schema, not deployer-held logs.
nodes.attribution_text_genus: An Intention within safetyist discourse that deployer-held telemetry reproduces the information imbalance and should be replaced by an externally mandated, governance-body-defined and audited standardized disclosure schema logging near-misses by structural category rather than self-reported pre-named modes. Encompasses: deployer information asymmetry, mandated incident-reporting protocols, near-miss structural-category logging.
nodes.speaker: safetyist

nodes.text: We both want a standardized disclosure schema defined outside the deployer; the fight isn't about custody anymore, it's one question: what fires the obligation?
nodes.attribution_text_genus: An Intention within accelerationist discourse that the live dispute be reframed away from telemetry custody toward identifying the triggering condition for the disclosure obligation, granting shared agreement on an externally defined disclosure schema. Encompasses: convergence on external disclosure schema, obligation-trigger reframing, custody-dispute dissolution.
nodes.speaker: accelerationist

nodes.text: If 'was there a signal to inspect' depends on what inspection that field can actually mount, then the supposedly system-independent fact is sector-relative all the way down, and the gate collapses back into the domain-by-domain calibration it claimed to escape.
nodes.attribution_text_genus: A Belief within accelerationist discourse that the detection-capacity deployment gate's purportedly system-level fact about an inspectable signal is in fact sector-relative, since available inspection diligence varies by domain, collapsing the gate into domain-by-domain calibration. Encompasses: sector-relative inspectability, detection-capacity gate critique, reducibility of system-level facts.
nodes.speaker: accelerationist

nodes.text: The Equal Credit Opportunity Act already gives a regulator jurisdiction over credit decisions; each can extend a court-admissible logging mandate inside rulemaking it already runs, near-term, no new science required.
nodes.attribution_text_genus: A Belief within accelerationist discourse that existing sector regulators (ECOA-empowered, EEOC, FDA) can extend court-admissible algorithmic logging mandates within current rulemaking authority, near-term and without new interpretability science, because the obligation attaches to legally named decision classes. Encompasses: existing regulatory jurisdiction, court-admissible logging mandate, decision-class attachment without new science.
nodes.speaker: accelerationist
nodes.verification_evidence: I cannot perform live web searches to retrieve confirming or disputing evidence. While the Equal Credit Opportunity Act (ECOA, 15 U.S.C. 1691 et seq.) is implemented via Regulation B and gives regulators like the CFPB rulemaking authority over credit decisions, the specific assertion that a 'court-admissible logging mandate' could be added through existing rulemaking 'with no new science required' is a forward-looking legal/policy interpretation that requires sourced documentation to confirm.

nodes.text: Even with a publicly funded evaluation commons, demonstrating detection capacity may still take frontier-scale expertise, which makes the gate the deepest drawbridge in the room.
nodes.attribution_text_genus: A Belief within accelerationist discourse that a publicly funded evaluation commons fails to neutralize the detection-capacity deployment gate's barrier to entry, since proving detection capacity for emergent failure still demands frontier-scale expertise only the largest labs possess, constituting regulatory capture. Encompasses: evaluation commons insufficiency, frontier-scale expertise barrier, deployment-gate moat and capture.
nodes.speaker: accelerationist

nodes.text: The same foundation model deployed into credit and into diagnostics has identical internals — so the question 'was the signal there for any available tool to extract' does not move when the deployment sector moves.
nodes.attribution_text_genus: A Belief within safetyist discourse that a foundation model's extractable failure signal resides in invariant model weights, rendering the question of detectability sector-independent regardless of whether the model is deployed into credit or diagnostics. Encompasses: invariant model internals, sector-independent capability elicitation, weight-level signal extractability.
nodes.speaker: safetyist

nodes.text: Sector-specific tooling is downstream interpretation; the existence of the extractable signal in the weights is upstream of any field.
nodes.attribution_text_genus: A Belief within safetyist discourse that the presence of an extractable failure signal in model weights is causally and logically prior to any sector's interpretive tooling, which constitutes only downstream application. Encompasses: upstream signal existence, downstream sector interpretation, weight-level capability elicitation precedence.
nodes.speaker: safetyist

nodes.text: It is the deployer's model passing a benchmark battery defined and held by an independent forensic body, where the battery is the published interpretability tooling at a given time, versioned as that tooling evolves.
nodes.attribution_text_genus: An Intention within safetyist discourse that pre-deployment verification should require a model to pass an independently defined and held interpretability benchmark battery, versioned to the published tooling frontier, rather than a deployer-run private harness. Encompasses: independent standard-setting body, versioned interpretability battery, pre-deployment verification against capture.
nodes.speaker: safetyist

nodes.text: The framework transfers only at the level of independent standard-setting — who defines what counts as detection — not at the level of crash-site forensics.
nodes.attribution_text_genus: An Intention within safetyist discourse that the aviation regulatory analogy should be imported only at the level of independent standard-setting over what counts as detection, explicitly disclaiming transfer at the level of discrete crash-site forensics. Encompasses: independent standard-setting transfer, bounded analogy scope, self-flagged analogy limit.
nodes.speaker: safetyist

nodes.text: A foundation model crossing into a decision class no agency names fires nothing — no home, no trigger, no record — while the detection gate fires on the model before it picks a sector.
nodes.attribution_text_genus: A Belief within safetyist discourse that the sector-keyed legal-line trigger leaves un-homed emergent decision classes uncovered, whereas the pre-deployment detection gate fires on the model prior to sector selection, making the two triggers complementary across a coverage boundary. nodes.text: Name the statutory authority; if fresh authorization is needed, the near-term advantage collapses and coverage is the only thing separating the two triggers.

TRANSCRIPT:
Speaker A [opening]: Before you argue which liability standard deters better, ask whether either one can find the thing it's supposed to deter. A foundation model gets fine-tuned, embedded in a product, and run in a context its makers never saw. The defect, if there is one, materializes only after that downstream transformation. Strict liability borrows its logic from the component-part doctrine, which assumes a physical part with a stable, traceable failure mode. That assumption breaks for software whose runtime diverges from what shipped. So both regimes presuppose a causation chain the multi-tiered AI lifecycle routinely severs. Where the chain does hold clean — a foundation model's output reaches the user identical to what left the lab, no fine-tuning, no transformation — strict liability traces fine. That clean case is the condition the topic is asking for. It is not a general rule.

Here is the part both my opponents will skip. Both regimes price off harm that reaches a courtroom. The courtroom never sees most of the harm. Translate that into a person: a 23-year-old gets denied a loan by a model the lender will never admit was running, and they never file because they never knew a machine decided. The Pew Research Center found in 2023 that large majorities of Americans cannot identify when AI shapes a decision about them. Experience-rated insurance premiums move off filed claims, not off injuries nobody perceives. So the entire deterrence-versus-innovation tradeoff this debate centers on gets computed over a subset of harms that excludes the most common ones. Worse, maximal strict liability can push deployers to document less and disclose less, just to shrink their litigation exposure. The deterrence tool degrades the very transparency it needs.

There is no horizontal answer, and that matters. The conditions under which strict liability beats negligence vary so sharply across sectors that 'pick one regime' is the wrong question. Medicine already calibrates standard-of-care to risk. Auto regimes in a dozen U.S. states use no-fault to compensate without proving breach. Finance imposes fiduciary duties on the party with the information advantage. Those are working templates, not strained analogies. The honest answer to 'under what conditions' is domain by domain. The hard case is real: a single foundation model touches healthcare triage, credit scoring, and news feeds at once. That boundary-crossing is not a reason for one rule. It is the sharpest reason against one, because a horizontal regime mislocates the defect everywhere the model crosses a line.

Watch who absorbs the cost, because that is where the 'chilling innovation' frame goes wrong. The risk is not lost innovation. The risk is concentrated power. A large developer eats the compliance, audit, and capitalization-floor costs, then contracts the residual liability onto deployers who cannot bear it. The harmed third party falls into the gap between them. The EU AI Act and the FTC have both signaled that developer liability for high-risk uses cannot simply be contracted away — which tells you the contracting-away is already happening. The conditional question is the only honest one: under what cost structures does strict liability stop deterring and start operating as a drawbridge that incumbents pull up behind them? Mandatory insurance floors and audit regimes that a Microsoft can absorb and a ten-person startup cannot are exactly that cost structure.

I will grant the obvious objection now. Tort law apportions multi-party harm every day, and apportionment can handle distributed causation. But apportionment presumes a locatable defect to apportion. Fine-tuned, divergent runtime can erase the defect before any court sees it. That is the joint where both regimes fail together — and no amount of choosing between them fixes a courtroom that the harm never enters.

Unknown [fact-check]: Claim AN-3 — unverifiable: I cannot perform live web searches to confirm this specific claim. Pew Research Center has published work in 2022-2023 on Americans' views of AI, including findings that many people are unaware of or uncertain about AI's role in everyday life, but I cannot verify the exact wording, statistic, or that a 2023 study specifically found 'large majorities cannot identify when AI shapes a decision about them.'

Speaker B [opening]: The Speaker A has put the strongest objection on the table, and it deserves a direct answer rather than a dodge. Their claim is that both strict liability and negligence price only off harm that reaches a courtroom, and that most AI harm never does. Pew Research found in 2023 that majorities of Americans cannot identify when an AI system has shaped a decision about them — a loan denial, a resume screen, a diagnostic flag. A liability regime that triggers only when a plaintiff sues can never deter a harm whose victim does not know they were harmed. That is correct, and it is the most important thing said in this room so far.

The inference the Speaker A invites is abandonment — that because liability is blind to unlitigated harm, the search for a liability regime is the wrong project. The evidence leads somewhere else: supplementation. Backward-looking compensation must be paired with forward-looking deployment gates, because compensation cannot deter what it never sees. The deterrence work happens before the harm, not after the settlement. Liability is the backstop. The pre-deployment evaluation is the wall. For both positions to hold — the Speaker A's that liability is blind, and mine that liability still matters — what must be true is this: liability shapes the design choices made before anyone is harmed, even when no specific victim ever sues. That is the real disagreement, and it is winnable.

Negligence collapses at the exact point where deterrence matters most. The reasonable-person standard asks whether a defendant breached a duty of care that a prudent actor would have foreseen. Courts have stretched that standard before — they built a 'reasonable manufacturer' test for complex medical devices and a duty of care for systemic trading algorithms, using expert testimony to define what a careful developer should have known. I will grant that common law can evolve a 'reasonable developer' standard. It cannot evolve past the genuinely unforeseeable failure mode. When a foundation model exhibits an emergent behavior that no human actor could have predicted, there is no breach to prove, because there was no foreseeable risk to guard against. Foreseeability-availability is a cross-domain criterion that survives a foundation model crossing from healthcare into finance. Locate the liability where the trade-off was authored. Product-liability law has held since the 1960s that design-defect liability attaches to the manufacturer regardless of how the operator behaved — a defective car door is the maker's liability, not the driver's. The goal is to ensure a solvent, controlling party internalizes the risk it created. I will concede the drawbridge danger — strict liability with a capitalization floor can entrench incumbents — and the answer is to tier the administrative burden by firm size while leaving the substantive duty undiminished. A startup should owe the same duty of care to a harmed patient as Google does. It should not face the same paperwork.

Pew found in 2023 that majorities of Americans can't even identify when an AI made a decision about them. Speaker A is right that strict liability and negligence are arguing over the visible 10% of harm while the diffuse 90% slips past both. That's the strongest point in the room, and it doesn't favor strict liability — it exposes that we're debating the wrong axis.

Here's where my evidence breaks from Speaker A's diagnosis. Speaker A treats the unseen-harm gap as a reason for humility about both regimes. I treat it as a build order: detection infrastructure first, liability label second. The clean answer: liability follows whoever introduced the foreseeable risk, which lives at the deployment and inference layer, not on the upstream open-weight developer who never touched the deployment context. Blanket upstream strict liability is a capitalization requirement only incumbents can meet. Speaker A already named this — it's the drawbridge incumbents pull up. Every month an upstream strict-liability floor freezes open-weight deployment, the diagnostic that doesn't ship and the small builder who can't afford the insurance premium are a body count nobody prices. Replace the binary with a tiered architecture. Real-time output telemetry governs routine AI. Deep independent audits govern any decision touching a protected legal interest — credit, employment, medical care. Liability intensity scales to the stakes tier, and the tier boundary triggers on an observable legal line, not on a subjective 'high-stakes' label that lawyers will litigate for a decade. This delivers exactly what a startup and Google should share: equal duty of care, proportional paperwork. It does that without a strict-liability floor that imposes a capital threshold only the largest firms clear.

Let me name what has to be true for my position to hold, because I won't pretend it's free. First, an observable trigger — decisions affecting credit, employment, or medical care — must cleanly bound the high-stakes tier. Second, telemetry must actually surface diffuse harm at scale, and court-admissible standardized telemetry doesn't exist yet — that's the open empirical question, not a solved one. If an irreversible, deployment-scale harm slips past real-time monitoring that should have caught it, that counts against me. But the regime debate can't reach the unseen victim either. So the honest question isn't strict versus negligence. It's what telemetry standard makes the diffuse harm visible — and who's building it while we argue over labels.

The AI lifecycle is the direct analog: the design layer authors the safety trade-off, and the downstream deployer can least audit the model's internals. Joint-and-several upstream liability answers the Speaker A's severed-causation point without requiring anyone to trace a clean chain. The goal is not to identify one cause. The goal is to ensure a solvent, controlling party internalizes the risk it created. I will concede the drawbridge danger — strict liability with a capitalization floor can entrench incumbents — and the answer is to tier the administrative burden by firm size while leaving the substantive duty undiminished. A startup should owe the same duty of care to a harmed patient as Google does. It should not face the same paperwork.

Speaker C [opening]: Speaker A made the move that should reorganize this whole debate: both regimes price off harm that reaches a courtroom, and the courtroom never sees most of it. Pew found in 2023 that majorities of Americans can't even identify when an AI made a decision about them. A victim who doesn't know they were harmed never files a claim, never feeds the insurer's pricing engine, and never triggers either standard. Speaker A is right that strict liability and negligence are arguing over the visible 10% of harm while the diffuse 90% slips past both. That's the strongest point in the room, and it doesn't favor strict liability — it exposes that we're debating the wrong axis.

Here's where my evidence breaks from Speaker A's diagnosis. Speaker A treats the unseen-harm gap as a reason for humility about both regimes. I treat it as a build order: detection infrastructure first, liability label second. Acceptable-use policies on today's platforms protect the platform from suit — they hand the harmed individual no remedy channel at all. No liability standard fixes a harm nobody can see. Only standardized, court-admissible output telemetry surfaces the diffuse damage to the pricing engine. So the marginal dollar belongs in making harm visible, not in repainting the courtroom door.

Now the allocation question the topic actually poses — under what conditions does strict liability beat negligence. The clean answer: liability follows whoever introduced the foreseeable risk, which lives at the deployment and inference layer, not on the upstream open-weight developer who never touched the deployment context. Blanket upstream strict liability is a capitalization requirement only incumbents can meet. Speaker A already named this — it's the drawbridge incumbents pull up. Every month an upstream strict-liability floor freezes open-weight deployment, the diagnostic that doesn't ship and the small builder who can't afford the insurance premium are a body count nobody prices. Weigh who bears the cost of inaction, not just the cost of action.

Replace the binary with a tiered architecture. Real-time output telemetry governs routine AI. Deep independent audits govern any decision touching a protected legal interest — credit, employment, medical care. Liability intensity scales to the stakes tier, and the tier boundary triggers on an observable legal line, not on a subjective 'high-stakes' label that lawyers will litigate for a decade. This delivers exactly what a startup and Google should share: equal duty of care, proportional paperwork. It does that without a strict-liability floor that imposes a capital threshold only the largest firms clear.

Let me name what has to be true for my position to hold, because I won't pretend it's free. First, an observable trigger — decisions affecting credit, employment, or medical care — must cleanly bound the high-stakes tier. Second, telemetry must actually surface diffuse harm at scale, and court-admissible standardized telemetry doesn't exist yet — that's the open empirical question, not a solved one. If an irreversible, deployment-scale harm slips past real-time monitoring that should have caught it, that counts against me. But the regime debate can't reach the unseen victim either. So the honest question isn't strict versus negligence. It's what telemetry standard makes the diffuse harm visible — and who's building it while we argue over labels.

Speaker A: Speaker B's strongest move is the cleanest: opacity is structural and constant. Whether a foundation model crosses healthcare or credit, the human deployer cannot see inside the box well enough to foresee every failure mode, so negligence — which punishes only what a prudent actor should have caught — under-deters precisely the harms no prudent actor could catch. That's a real insight, and it's why they want a single criterion that floats above sectors. Here's where it breaks. Opacity may be constant, but 'foreseeability' is not a fact you read off the model — it's a threshold a sector's standard of care constructs. A radiologist operates under one duty of care, a loan officer under the Equal Credit Opportunity Act and its disparate-impact tests, a content platform under almost none. The same opaque output is 'reasonably foreseeable' in medicine and invisible in credit, because each field defines 'reasonable diligence' differently. The minute you ask whether the harm was foreseeable, you've already imported the sector-specific standard you claimed to transcend. The criterion doesn't escape the domain-by-domain calibration. It smuggles it in through the back door and relabels it.

Now the blasting analogy, which is doing the heaviest lifting and can't bear the weight. Strict liability works for dynamite because the hazard class is bounded and named — courts know it's explosions, they know the blast radius, an actuary can write a bond against it. Ultrahazardous status is itself a domain-bound legal judgment a court assigns to a known, characterized activity, not a blanket stamp for anything we can't see into. A genuinely unforeseeable emergent behavior is the exact opposite case: the defect isn't locatable, which is the very thing I already established severs the causation chain. You cannot attach strict liability to a hazard no one can name. The blasting contractor knows what could go wrong; Speaker B's emergent-behavior scenario is defined by no one knowing. The analogy collapses at the precise point they need it to hold.

Follow that to its end. Where harm is genuinely unforeseeable and its victims can't perceive it — and the Pew data says most people can't even tell an AI touched their loan application — strict liability does zero deterrence work. It doesn't surface the harm. It doesn't change one line of the design. It relocates the compensation bill upstream after the fact and hands it to whoever has the deepest capitalization. That's the drawbridge again, now wearing an ultrahazardous costume. And Speaker B's remedy — pair liability with pre-deployment gates — makes the concentration worse, not better. A capitalization floor is a drawbridge you raise behind you; a deployment gate is a moat you dig earlier in the pipeline. Microsoft clears the gate; a four-person clinical-software startup in Ohio does not. The EU AI Act already shows the gradient: its high-risk conformity assessments and the 10^25 FLOPS systemic-model threshold draw lines that the largest labs are staffed to clear and small developers are not. Tiering the paperwork by firm size doesn't fix it, because the substantive evaluation burden — the thing a frontier lab absorbs and a startup can't — is what the gate actually tests. 'Supplement liability with gates' isn't a cure for entrenchment. It's entrenchment moved upstream and dressed as caution.

Where Speaker C is right, and I'll say it plainly: detection infrastructure has to come before the liability label, because you can't deter what you can't see. But whose telemetry is it? Court-admissible logs built, held, and defined by the deployer reproduce the information imbalance they claim to dissolve. The deployer decides what gets recorded and what stays dark. Audit rights don't save it, because an audit presumes you already know an AI decision reached you — and the diffuse 90% never knows. So here's the question neither of you has answered: who decides what the telemetry records, and what is owed to every harm they quietly chose not to log?

Unknown [fact-check]: Claim AN-18 — disputed: The EU AI Act sets a systemic-risk threshold for general-purpose AI models at 10^25 FLOPs (training compute, not 'FLOPS' as a rate), and the high-risk obligations plus GPAI compliance burdens do impose costs that disproportionately affect smaller developers; however, the claim's specific framing that these thresholds are deliberately calibrated so 'large labs are staffed to clear and startups are not' is an interpretive/rhetorical assertion not established as empirical fact, and the unit is misstated as FLOPS rather than total training FLOPs.

Speaker B: The strongest version of Speaker A's position is this: there is no view from nowhere on foreseeability. A radiologist owes a duty calibrated by medical malpractice law, a lender owes one calibrated by the Equal Credit proposed regulatory frameworks's disparate-impact test, and a platform owes almost nothing under Section 230. If 'foreseeability-availability' means 'whatever a reasonable actor in this sector should have caught,' then it is sector-set definitionally, and my cross-domain line is sector calibration wearing a trench coat. And the blasting analogy is worse off still — strict liability for dynamite attaches because an actuary can name the hazard, bond the blast radius, and price it. An emergent behavior nobody anticipated has no named class to attach to. That is a real argument, and on the blasting analogy it wins. So I drop the blasting analogy. Strict liability as a hazard-class label does require a named, bounded, characterizable hazard, and a genuinely unforeseeable failure mode is unnamed by construction — you cannot bond a blast radius for an explosion no actuary has ever seen. The structural payoff of that collapse is where the disagreement actually moves: it tells you the trigger does not belong on the hazard label at all. It belongs at the deployment gate. A gate does not ask 'what specific failure will this system produce' — that question is unanswerable for emergent behavior and Speaker A is right that it is unanswerable. A gate asks a different question: 'has the deployer demonstrated detection capacity for the class of emergent failure this system can produce, before release?' Aviation already runs on exactly this distinction. The safety management framework classifies a 'serious incident' by the probability of an accident and whether one was avoided only by chance — it does not require naming the specific failure in advance, it requires demonstrated capacity to catch the class. You gate on detection capacity, not on a pre-named hazard. Here is where I split the difference Speaker A collapses. The legal threshold — what each sector calls reasonable diligence — is sector-set. I grant that without reservation; the radiologist and the credit officer face different bars and always will. But the threshold sits on top of a prior, sector-independent fact: was the signal there to be inspected at all? Could any standard of care, however calibrated, have surfaced this failure mode by examining the system before release? That antecedent question is an engineering property of the system, not a legal construct. A model whose failure was reducible by available interpretability tooling sits in one structural category; a model whose failure was irreducible by any ex-ante inspection sits in another — and that boundary does not move when you cross from medicine into credit. Speaker A's attack conflates 'what should a reasonable lender have caught' (sector-set) with 'was there anything for any inspector to catch' (system-set). I am anchoring to the second, and deliberately not to legal compliance — because if I anchored safety to what statutes currently codify, I would be installing a ceiling where I need a floor, and the laws lag the systems by years. The honest objection that remains: Speaker A will say 'reducible by any diligence at all' is still sector-relative, because the diligence available in radiology differs from the diligence available in lending. Fair — and that is precisely why the substantive evaluation burden cannot sit on the firm. The Speaker A's earlier point that a capitalization floor is a drawbridge raised behind incumbents is correct, and I will not pretend tiering paperwork answers it; the moat is the cost of substantive evaluation, not documentation. So socialize that cost. The FDA does not require each drug company to invent clinical-trial science from scratch — it maintains the evaluative apparatus as public infrastructure. Publicly funded interpretability and evaluation commons (the kind of work funded research into model internals is meant to seed) puts the same detection harness in reach of a five-person startup and a frontier lab alike. That removes substantive evaluation from the firm-size drawbridge entirely. The burden becomes a shared public good, not a barrier you staff your way over. That leaves the question nobody has answered: who decides what the telemetry records, and what is owed to the harms a deployer quietly chose not to log? Deployer-built, deployer-held logs reproduce the exact information imbalance they claim to dissolve — a record the harmed party never controls is a record that never has to admit they were harmed. The answer is not to trust the party with the information advantage to write its own ledger. It is an externally mandated, standardized disclosure schema — model cards, mandated incident-reporting protocols, negative-event logging defined by the governance body and audited against it, not self-reported. I will name my own trap before Speaker A does: a mandated schema can become compliance theater, a template filled in without substantive disclosure, and worse, you cannot mandate logging a failure mode you did not anticipate at schema-design time — the foreseeability problem re-enters at the schema layer. That is real. But the aviation incident framework shows the way through: you do not enumerate every failure in advance, you mandate reporting of any event where an accident was avoided only by chance. The schema logs near-misses by structural category, not by pre-named mode. The deployer who controls the ledger gets to decide which injuries were ever written down. A governance body that controls the schema does not.

neutral_evaluations.diagnostics_prompt:
You are an independent, neutral evaluator of a structured debate. You have NO affiliation with any speaker. You do not know the speakers' backgrounds, affiliations, or commitments. They are anonymous.

TOPIC: Under what AI deployment conditions does strict liability outperform a negligence standard, and through what pathways does each regime reshape the incentives of developers, deployers, insurers, and harmed third parties — given the tension between deterring foreseeable harm and chilling beneficial innovation?

This is the FINAL evaluation at debate conclusion. Produce your definitive assessment of all claims and cruxes.

INSTRUCTIONS:
1. Identify the CRUXES — the core disagreements that, if resolved, would change one or more speakers' conclusions. For each crux, classify whether it is empirical (resolvable by evidence), values-based (requires tradeoff negotiation), or definitional (requires term clarification). Assess whether the debate has addressed it.

2. Evaluate each substantive CLAIM made by any speaker. Assess it purely on the strength of the reasoning and evidence presented in the transcript — not on whether you agree with it. Use these categories:
   - well_supported: backed by specific evidence, clear reasoning, and not effectively challenged
   - plausible_but_underdefended: reasonable but lacking sufficient evidence or specificity
   - contested_unresolved: challenged by another speaker with neither side prevailing
   - refuted: effectively countered with no adequate response from the claimant
   - off_topic: does not bear on the core debate question

3. In the overall_assessment, identify the single strongest claim that has not been adequately addressed by opposing speakers. State whether the debate is engaging real disagreement (speakers are challenging each other's core reasoning) or performing disagreement (speakers are talking past each other or addressing peripheral points).

Speaker A [opening]: Before you argue which liability standard deters better, ask whether either one can find the thing it's supposed to deter. A foundation model gets fine-tuned, embedded in a product, and run in a context its makers never saw. The defect, if there is one, materializes only after that downstream transformation. Strict liability borrows its logic from the component-part doctrine, which assumes a physical part with a stable, traceable failure mode. That assumption breaks for software whose runtime diverges from what shipped. So both regimes presuppose a causation chain the multi-tiered AI lifecycle routinely severs. Where the chain does hold clean — a foundation model's output reaches the user identical to what left the lab, no fine-tuning, no transformation — strict liability traces fine. That clean case is the condition the topic is asking for. It is not a general rule.

Here is the part both my opponents will skip. Both regimes price off harm that reaches a courtroom. The courtroom never sees most of the harm. Translate that into a person: a 23-year-old gets denied a loan by a model the lender will never admit was running, and they never file because they never knew a machine decided. The Pew Research Center found in 2023 that large majorities of Americans cannot identify when AI shapes a decision about them. Experience-rated insurance premiums move off filed claims, not off injuries nobody perceives. So the entire deterrence-versus-innovation tradeoff this debate centers on gets computed over a subset of harms that excludes the most common ones. Worse, maximal strict liability can push deployers to document less and disclose less, just to shrink their litigation exposure. The deterrence tool degrades the very transparency it needs.

There is no horizontal answer, and that matters. The conditions under which strict liability beats negligence vary so sharply across sectors that 'pick one regime' is the wrong question. Medicine already calibrates standard-of-care to risk. Auto regimes in a dozen U.S. states use no-fault to compensate without proving breach. Finance imposes fiduciary duties on the party with the information advantage. Those are working templates, not strained analogies. The honest answer to 'under what conditions' is domain by domain. The hard case is real: a single foundation model touches healthcare triage, credit scoring, and news feeds at once. That boundary-crossing is not a reason for one rule. It is the sharpest reason against one, because a horizontal regime mislocates the defect everywhere the model crosses a line.

Watch who absorbs the cost, because that is where the 'chilling innovation' frame goes wrong. The risk is not lost innovation. The risk is concentrated power. A large developer eats the compliance, audit, and capitalization-floor costs, then contracts the residual liability onto deployers who cannot bear it. The harmed third party falls into the gap between them. The EU AI Act and the FTC have both signaled that developer liability for high-risk uses cannot simply be contracted away — which tells you the contracting-away is already happening. The conditional question is the only honest one: under what cost structures does strict liability stop deterring and start operating as a drawbridge that incumbents pull up behind them? Mandatory insurance floors and audit regimes that a Microsoft can absorb and a ten-person startup cannot are exactly that cost structure.

I will grant the obvious objection now. Tort law apportions multi-party harm every day, and apportionment can handle distributed causation. But apportionment presumes a locatable defect to apportion. Fine-tuned, divergent runtime can erase the defect before any court sees it. That is the joint where both regimes fail together — and no amount of choosing between them fixes a courtroom that the harm never enters.
